lead: This unit studies second order partial differential equations that model waves, heat flow and steady potentials. You learn to factor constant-coefficient equations, classify them, separate variables, and build Fourier series solutions for standard boundary value problems. After it you can solve the common exam models and read the physics behind each condition.
about: The unit moves from algebraic solution to physical models. Chapter 5.1 solves linear homogeneous PDEs with constant coefficients by factoring the operator into first order factors and adding arbitrary functions. Chapter 5.2 classifies second order equations as elliptic, parabolic or hyperbolic using a discriminant, so you know which model you face. Chapter 5.3 introduces separation of variables, the engine for the rest. Chapters 5.4 to 5.6 apply it to the wave equation, heat equation and Laplace equation in Cartesian and polar coordinates. Chapter 5.7 closes the loop: Fourier series fit initial and boundary data, turning product solutions into full solutions. Each chapter uses ODE results from earlier units and stops where another unit owns the topic.

chapters.idea: Constant-coefficient linear homogeneous PDEs can be solved by factoring the differential operator into first order factors and adding arbitrary functions.
chapters.depth: Cover equations A u_xx + B u_xy + C u_yy + ... = 0 with constant coefficients, where subscripts mean partial derivatives. Factor the operator using D=∂/∂x and D'=∂/∂y, solve each first order factor, and sum arbitrary functions. Include repeated factors and higher order factors. Some syllabi call this the complementary function of a linear PDE. Keep to constant coefficients; variable coefficients belong elsewhere.

figure.title: Operator factoring
figure.aria: A block diagram shows a constant-coefficient PDE factored into first order pieces, each solved and then added as arbitrary functions.

chapters.example: Solve u_xx − 5u_xy + 6u_yy = 0. Factor as (D−2D′)(D−3D′)u=0. The first factor gives u=f(y+2x) and the second gives u=g(y+3x). General solution: u=f(y+2x)+g(y+3x) for arbitrary twice differentiable f and g.
chapters.trap: Treating arbitrary functions as constants, or missing the x multiplier for a repeated factor.
chapters.prereq: Unit 4 for PDE notation; Unit 2 for linear ODEs with constant coefficients.
chapters.leave: Classification and boundary value solutions; nonlinear first order PDE methods stay in Unit 4.

chapters.idea: A second order linear PDE in two variables is elliptic, parabolic or hyperbolic according to the sign of its discriminant.
chapters.depth: For A u_xx + B u_xy + C u_yy + lower terms = 0, compute Δ=B²−4AC at a point. Δ<0 elliptic, Δ=0 parabolic, Δ>0 hyperbolic. Show Laplace, heat and wave as prototypes. Mention variable coefficients can change type. Some books write the mixed term as 2B u_xy; then the test is B²−AC. Only a few universities ask for canonical form reduction.

figure.aria: A decision tree tests the discriminant B squared minus 4AC and sends the equation to elliptic, parabolic or hyperbolic.

chapters.example: Classify u_xx + 4u_xy + 3u_yy = 0. Here A=1, B=4, C=3, so B²−4AC=16−12=4>0. The equation is hyperbolic.
chapters.trap: Using B²−4AC when the equation is written with 2B u_xy; then use B²−AC. Also check coefficients after moving all terms to one side.
chapters.prereq: Unit 4 for forming PDEs and partial derivative notation.
chapters.leave: Solving methods for each type; canonical forms unless taught.

chapters.idea: Assume a product solution so a PDE splits into ordinary differential equations linked by one separation constant.
chapters.depth: Assume u=X(x)Y(y) or u=X(x)T(t). Substitute, divide by XY, set each side equal to a separation constant λ. Solve the resulting ODEs and impose homogeneous boundary conditions to get eigenvalues and eigenfunctions. Superpose products. Some syllabi call this the product method or Fourier method. Keep to two independent variables.

figure.title: Separation route
figure.aria: A left-to-right flow shows a PDE turned into a product, split by a constant into two ODEs, then solved for eigenfunctions.

chapters.example: Find product solutions of u_xx + u_yy = 0 with separation constant 4. Put u=X(x)Y(y). Then X″/X = −Y″/Y = 4, so X″−4X=0 and Y″+4Y=0. Thus u=(A e^{2x}+B e^{−2x})(C cos 2y+D sin 2y).
chapters.trap: Choosing the sign of λ so the boundary conditions cannot be met; for zero ends use sine in that direction, which needs a negative constant there.
chapters.prereq: Unit 2 for second order ODEs; Unit 4 for PDE notation.
chapters.leave: Full Fourier coefficients and physical boundary conditions to 5.4–5.7.

chapters.idea: The wave equation has two traveling-wave families, and D'Alembert's formula combines them from initial position and velocity.
chapters.depth: Cover u_tt=c²u_xx, where c is wave speed. Use characteristics ξ=x−ct, η=x+ct to get u=F(x−ct)+G(x+ct). For an infinite string with initial displacement f and velocity g, use u=½[f(x−ct)+f(x+ct)] + 1/(2c)∫_{x−ct}^{x+ct}g(s)ds. Mention finite string reflections and boundary conditions, solved by Fourier series in 5.7. Some syllabi call this the vibrating string equation.

figure.title: D'Alembert split
figure.aria: Initial wave data splits into a right-moving wave and a left-moving wave, which are added, with a velocity integral included.

chapters.example: Solve u_tt=4u_xx on the whole line, with u(x,0)=sin x and u_t(x,0)=0. Here c=2. D'Alembert gives u=½[sin(x−2t)+sin(x+2t)]. Using sin A+sin B=2 sin((A+B)/2)cos((A−B)/2), u=sin x cos 2t.
chapters.trap: Dropping the factor 1/(2c) in the velocity integral, or using x+ct and x−ct with the wrong sign. D'Alembert is for an infinite line; a finite string needs boundary series.
chapters.prereq: Chapter 2 classification, Chapter 3 separation, Unit 2 ODEs.
chapters.leave: Finite string Fourier solution to 5.7; numerical wave methods elsewhere.

chapters.idea: The heat equation smooths temperature by decaying sine modes in time.
chapters.depth: Cover u_t=α²u_xx for a rod, where α² is thermal diffusivity. Explain Dirichlet (fixed temperature) and insulated (zero flux) ends. Separate u=X(x)T(t) to get sine/cosine modes and time decay e^{−α²n²π²t/L²}. Include steady state when ends are fixed at different temperatures. Some syllabi call this the diffusion equation.

figure.aria: Two sine-shaped temperature profiles show the initial peak at 100 and a lower later profile after heat diffusion.

chapters.example: Solve u_t=u_xx for 0, t>0, with u(0,t)=u(π,t)=0 and u(x,0)=100 sin x. Try u=e^{−λt}sin x. Then u_t=−λu and u_xx=−u, so −λ=−1, λ=1. Solution: u=100 e^{−t}sin x.
chapters.trap: Using α instead of α²; forgetting the n² in the decay exponent; using sine modes when the ends are insulated (use cosine).
chapters.prereq: Chapter 3 separation; Unit 2 ODEs; Fourier series in 5.7 for general initial data.
chapters.leave: General Fourier coefficients to 5.7; numerical heat methods elsewhere.

chapters.idea: Laplace's equation gives steady potentials, solved by separation in rectangles and in disks.
chapters.depth: Write Laplace's equation as u_xx+u_yy=0 in Cartesian coordinates and u_rr+(1/r)u_r+(1/r²)u_θθ=0 in polar coordinates. Solve rectangles with products of sine/cosine and sinh/cosh. Solve disks with r^n cos nθ, r^n sin nθ; reject r^{−n} at the origin. Boundary data is fitted by Fourier series in 5.7. Some syllabi call it the potential equation.

figure.title: Laplace choices
figure.aria: Laplace's equation branches into Cartesian and polar separation, with the polar branch rejecting singular r to the minus n terms before fitting boundary data.

chapters.example: Solve ∇²u=0 inside the disk r<2, with u(2,θ)=cos 2θ and u finite at r=0. A bounded harmonic solution is u=r²(A cos 2θ+B sin 2θ). At r=2, 4A cos 2θ+4B sin 2θ=cos 2θ, so A=1/4, B=0. Thus u=(r²/4)cos 2θ.
chapters.trap: Dropping 1/r or 1/r² in the polar Laplacian; keeping a term that blows up at the origin; using the wrong power of the boundary radius.
chapters.prereq: Chapter 3 separation; Unit 2 ODEs; Fourier series for general boundary data in 5.7.
chapters.leave: Fourier coefficients to 5.7; complex variable methods and Green's functions are outside this unit.

chapters.idea: Fourier series use orthogonality to fit initial or boundary data, turning separated modes into the required solution.
chapters.depth: Cover Fourier sine and cosine series on 0, half-range expansions, and the coefficient formulas. Use orthogonality to fit initial temperature or string shape. Put the coefficients into the mode solutions from 5.4–5.6. Work through one heat and one wave example. State convergence at jumps only briefly. Some syllabi call this the Fourier method for boundary value problems.

figure.title: Fourier fitting
figure.aria: A flow shows boundary data projected onto Fourier coefficients, inserted into mode solutions, and summed into the full series.

chapters.example: Solve u_t=u_xx for 0, t>0, with u(0,t)=u(1,t)=0 and u(x,0)=100. The sine series is u=Σ b_n e^{−n²π²t} sin(nπx), with b_n=2∫_0^1 100 sin(nπx)dx. This gives b_n=0 for even n and b_n=400/(nπ) for odd n. Hence u=Σ_{n odd} 400/(nπ)e^{−n²π²t}sin(nπx).
chapters.trap: Using 1/L instead of 2/L in the half-range sine coefficient; mixing sine and cosine modes; forgetting the exponential time factor for heat or the cosine time factor for wave.
chapters.leave: Sturm-Liouville theory and convergence proofs to Unit 3.
